pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, What Causes Wind — the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly, warm air rises because it is lighter, and cooler air flows in to take its place; that moving air is wind.
• Standards — UK (DfE): builds toward KS2 states/forces and KS3 atmosphere; at KS1/KS2 it sits within weather observation rather than a discrete statutory objective.
• Standards — US (NGSS): the convection mechanism is formalised later (MS-ESS2-6 role of unequal heating in atmospheric circulation; energy transfer in MS-PS3); at grade 3 it grounds 3-ESS2-1 weather description. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach wind as a CONSEQUENCE of uneven heating and rising warm air, not a mysterious push; use the sea-breeze case (land heats faster than sea) as the canonical concrete example; make the invisible visible via effects (streamers, smoke) and a convection cross-section; keep 'warm air rises, cool air moves in' as the core causal chain.
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — state that the Sun heats the surface unevenly and define wind as moving air; Tier B — explain warm air rises and cool air flows in to replace it (a convection loop); Tier C — relate pressure differences to wind direction and strength.
bestPractices: Anchor to the sea breeze: land heats faster than the sea, air rises over the warm land, cooler sea air flows in — a concrete, everyday convection loop
Make wind visible through its effects (streamers, smoke traces, a pinwheel) since air itself is invisible
Teach the full causal chain 'uneven heating → warm air rises → cool air rushes in = wind' rather than a single fact
Use a convection cross-section (arrows up over warm, down over cool, sideways as wind) as the canonical model
Confront the idea that wind is created by trees/waves moving or comes from a fixed place — those are effects, not causes
keyRepresentations: Convection-loop cross-section: rising arrows over warm ground, sinking over cool, horizontal flow labelled 'wind'
Sea-breeze diagram (sun, warm land, cool sea, incoming breeze)
A heat dial that speeds/slows the rising air and the resulting sideways flow
Streamers/smoke traces revealing invisible moving air
commonMisconceptions: Wind is made by trees swaying, waves, or fans — those show or move air but the driver is uneven heating
Wind 'comes from' a fixed place or is a substance stored somewhere, rather than air flowing to replace risen warm air
Warm air sinks / cold air rises (reversed) — warm air is lighter and rises
Wind and the air are different things — wind IS moving air
Heating happens evenly, so there'd be no reason for air to move

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach wind as a consequence of uneven solar heating: the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly, warm air is lighter and rises, and cooler air flows in to take its place — that moving air IS the wind. Anchor to the sea breeze (land heats faster than sea) as the canonical concrete example, make the invisible air visible through its effects (streamers, smoke, a pinwheel), and teach the full causal chain rather than a single fact. Confront the common belief that wind is 'made by' trees or waves, or that it is a special substance separate from air.

activities.title: Sea-breeze convection playground
feedback: If the learner says the trees or waves make the wind: trees and waves move BECAUSE of the wind — wind also blows over open sea where there are no trees or hills at all.
If the learner says warm air sinks: warm air is lighter and rises — think of the warmth you feel rising above a radiator, or a hot-air balloon climbing.
If the learner treats wind as separate from air: a fan or a wave of your hand turns still air into a breeze you can feel — wind IS air in motion.
When the breeze dies as the heat is turned down: point out that without uneven heating there is nothing to make the air move, so there is no wind from this cause.
When the night-time breeze reverses: the land is now cooler than the sea, so warm air rises over the sea and cooler land air flows out to replace it — the loop runs the other way.
activities.rationale: Wind causation is a convection mechanism; letting the child drive the heating and watch warm air rise while cooler air visibly flows in makes the abstract chain 'air moves to replace risen warm air' observable and controllable. The heat dial and reversible day/night cases let the learner test cause and effect rather than accept an asserted arrow.
sourceClaims: Uneven solar heating drives convection: warm air rises and cooler air moves in to replace it, producing wind; the sea breeze (land heats faster than sea) is the canonical example.
Children commonly attribute wind to moving objects (trees, waves) or treat it as a substance from a fixed source, rather than as air flowing due to heating differences.
learnerActions: Look at a cross-section showing the Sun, warm land, cool sea, and the air above
Warm the land using a Sun/heat control and watch a column of warm air rise over the land
Watch streamers (or smoke traces) reveal cooler sea air streaming sideways to fill the gap left by the risen warm air — and name that sideways flow as the wind
Turn the heat UP and observe the breeze strengthen; turn it DOWN and watch the breeze die away
Switch to a cool night where the land cools faster than the sea, and observe the breeze reverse direction; explain why
activities.intendedInsight: Wind is not a mysterious push and is not made by trees or waves — it is simply air moving to replace warm air that rose because the Sun heated the surface unevenly. Changing the heating changes the wind; removing the uneven heating stops it.

activities.title: Make the invisible air visible
feedback: If the learner thinks nothing is moving because they cannot see it: the streamer/pinwheel moves because invisible air is pushing against it.
Connect the observed flow to its cause: the air is moving toward where warm air has risen and left a gap.
activities.rationale: Because air is invisible, concrete indicators MAY help learners perceive that something is actually moving, which can support the shift from treating wind as a stored substance from a fixed source toward seeing it as air in motion. This perceptual benefit is an unvalidated proposal, not a source-established finding; source claim 3 is cited only because it documents the misconception this activity targets.
sourceClaims: Children commonly attribute wind to moving objects (trees, waves) or treat it as a substance from a fixed source, rather than as air flowing due to heating differences.
learnerActions: Use streamers, smoke traces, or a pinwheel to detect moving air you cannot see
Observe which way the indicators point and describe the direction and strength of the air movement
Relate what the indicators show back to warm air rising somewhere and cooler air flowing in
activities.intendedInsight: Air itself is invisible, but its movement can be detected through its effects — and those effects are evidence of air flowing, which is what wind is.

activities.title: Order the causal chain and explain the sea breeze
feedback: If the order is muddled: start from what the Sun does first (heats the surface unevenly) and follow what happens to the air step by step.
For the night case: the land is now the cooler surface, so the rising happens over the sea and air flows out from the land — the breeze reverses.

For the open ocean: wind still occurs because the Sun heats different parts of the Earth (sea, land, near and far) by different amounts, so air keeps moving, and that moving air can travel far across the ocean; trees and hills are not needed.
activities.rationale: Ordering the chain and explaining the sea breeze checks whether the learner can sequence and apply the mechanism; the night-time and open-ocean prompts discriminate genuine understanding from a memorised single fact. An ordering task checks that the learner can sequence the chain but does not by itself build dynamic intuition, so it works best after hands-on or observed exploration.
sourceClaims: Uneven solar heating drives convection: warm air rises and cooler air moves in to replace it, producing wind; the sea breeze (land heats faster than sea) is the canonical example.
learnerActions: Arrange the steps of the causal chain in order: uneven heating → warm air rises → cooler air moves in → wind
In your own words, explain why a breeze often blows from the sea onto the land on a hot afternoon
Predict and explain which way the breeze blows at night when the land cools faster than the sea
Decide whether there could be wind over the open ocean with no trees or hills, and say what causes it
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can state and apply the full chain of causes, not just recite that wind exists, and can use it to predict wind direction in new situations.

activities.title: Ask a weather expert why the wind blows
feedback: If the retelling drops a step, point to the missing link (what makes the air rise, or what fills the gap).
If the learner says equal heating would still make wind: with no uneven heating there is no reason for air to rise and be replaced, so there would be little or no wind from this cause.
activities.rationale: A spoken or written explanation lets the learner articulate the mechanism and tackle a counterfactual (equal heating), which targets the misconception that heating is even. This supports verbal reasoning alongside the observed model rather than replacing hands-on exploration; a narrated account alone does not let the learner see the loop in motion.
sourceClaims: Uneven solar heating drives convection: warm air rises and cooler air moves in to replace it, producing wind; the sea breeze (land heats faster than sea) is the canonical example.
learnerActions: Pose the question 'why does the wind blow?' and listen to or read an explanation that narrates uneven heating, rising warm air, and cooler air moving in
Retell the chain back and ask a follow-up, such as what would happen if the Sun heated everywhere equally
activities.intendedInsight: The same causal chain can be put into words and reasoned about in dialogue, reinforcing the explanation the learner has observed.

constraints: Target age is 7–9. Keep to 'uneven heating → warm air rises → cooler air moves in = wind' as the core chain; relating pressure differences to wind direction/strength is an extension (upper tier), not required for all learners.

A static labelled convection diagram names the parts but cannot show the air flowing; use it as a reference scaffold and pair it with moving indicators or an animated/manipulable model so the 'rushes in to replace' step is seen, not just asserted.
Step-ordering or matching tasks check that the learner can sequence the chain but do not on their own build the dynamic intuition of why air moves; use them after hands-on or observed exploration.
A 3D rendering of the convection cell is not required: the mechanism reads clearly in a 2D vertical cross-section. Offer 3D only if it adds clarity, not as a necessity.

Streamers, smoke, pinwheels and heat controls are offered as example mechanisms for revealing invisible flow and driving the heating; any means that makes the flow observable and the heating adjustable serves the same purpose.
Keep the direction of convection correct: warm air is lighter and RISES; cooler, denser air flows in. Watch for and correct the inverted 'warm air sinks' idea.

Keep the sea-/land-breeze reversal consistent: by day land heats faster so air rises over the land and sea air flows in; by night land cools faster so air rises over the warmer sea and land air flows out.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the listed sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
All three source claims are marked verified:false in the original row; treat the convection account, the NGSS grade mapping, and the misconceptions literature as unconfirmed citations.

The explanation 'warm air rises because it is lighter' is a simplified, age-appropriate account of buoyancy/density differences; it is correct at this level but omits that warm air is less dense. Acceptable for ages 7–9.

Original artefact ratings asserted that a 2D interactive is 'ideal', that 3D 'adds little', and that a static diagram 'cannot show' the flow; these are catalog preferences, not established efficacy claims, and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits here.
The claim about NGSS placement (MS-ESS2-6 vs 3-ESS2-1) is a standards-mapping note from the pedagogy field and was not used to make pedagogical-necessity claims.

Whether concrete flow indicators (streamers/pinwheels) improve understanding is an unvalidated pedagogical proposal; source claim 3 only establishes that the 'wind is a stored substance/moving-object' misconception exists, not that these indicators remediate it.

probeDeeper: At night the land cools faster than the sea. Which way would the breeze blow then — and why?
Where is the air going when it 'rises' over the warm land?
Could there be wind over the open ocean with no trees or hills anywhere? What causes it?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun heats the land more than the sea; air over the warm land warms, becomes lighter and rises; cooler, denser air from over the sea flows in to take its place — that moving air is the wind. Wind is air moving because of uneven heating, from cooler/denser toward warmer/rising air.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Trees and waves make the wind by swishing about'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reverse it — trees move BECAUSE of wind; wind blows over open sea with no trees at all.
errorPatterns.distractor: The trees and waves swishing about push the air and make the wind.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names moving objects as the cause of wind

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Wind is its own special thing, not just moving air'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A fan or hand-wave turns still air into felt wind — wind IS moving air.
errorPatterns.distractor: Wind is a kind of invisible thing that isn't the same as air.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can't say wind is air in motion

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Warm air sinks and cool air rises' — inverted convection
errorPatterns.nextMove: Warm air rises — show warmth above a radiator / a rising warm balloon.
errorPatterns.distractor: The warm air over the land sinks and pushes the breeze out to sea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gets the direction of rising air wrong

responseLevels.gap: Attributes wind to trees/waves or calls it a special substance.
responseLevels.full: Explains the sea breeze via uneven heating, rising warm air and cooler air flowing in, and predicts the reversed night-time land breeze.
responseLevels.partial: Says wind is moving air and heat is involved but cannot chain uneven heating → warm air rises → cooler air moves in, or gets the convection direction wrong.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: At the seaside on a hot afternoon a breeze often blows in from the sea onto the land. What makes the air move — what is wind, really?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks wind is 'made by trees/waves' or is special stuff cannot explain the sea breeze; only the uneven-heating → rising-air → air-moves-in model explains why the breeze blows from sea to land on a hot day.
